name: unsupported_mechanism
source: rubric/live review: rationale adds "saturated tails lack double bonds" not in the explanation
known_defect: Key and rationale add a bend angle and a claim about saturated tails that the explanation never states.

support_quotes: They form a bilayer with heads toward water on both sides and tails tucked inside.
Phospholipids have water-loving heads and water-avoiding tails: this combination is called amphipathic.

issues.detail: The explanation says double bonds kink tails and make packing harder; it gives no 30-degree bend and does not say what saturated tails lack.

support_quotes: Fluidity describes how freely membrane components move.
Tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol affect it.
Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains movement when the membrane is very fluid and prevents excessive stiffening in the cold.
The fluid mosaic model describes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways.
The two membrane layers, or leaflets, differ in composition.
Lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases.
Sugars on the outer surface form the glycocalyx and help cells recognize one another, including distinguishing self from non-self.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement fits both the water-loving heads and water-avoiding tails of phospholipids?

options.a: Heads face water; tails face inward.
options.b: Heads face inward; tails face water.
options.c: Heads and tails both face water.
options.d: Heads and tails both face inward.

questions.prompt: A student calls a phospholipid entirely water-loving because its head likes water. Which description matches the whole molecule?

options.a: Its head and tails both avoid water.
options.b: Its head and tails both like water.
options.c: Its head likes water; its tails avoid water.
options.d: Its head avoids water; its tails like water.

questions.prompt: Why do unsaturated tails increase fluidity?

options.a: Rigid bends in the tails create gaps that keep them from packing closely.
options.b: Their tails bind to cholesterol and are held in place.
options.c: Their heads pull the tails closer together.
options.d: Their tails are shorter than saturated tails.

questions.prompt: Two membranes contain the same kinds of components, but those components move more freely in membrane A. Which is more fluid?

options.a: Membrane B, because less movement means greater fluidity.
options.b: Both equally, because movement does not define fluidity.
options.c: Neither, because fluidity describes composition instead of movement.
options.d: Membrane A, because greater movement means greater fluidity.

questions.prompt: The explanation lists chain length as a fluidity factor but gives no direction. Can it alone support a prediction about shorter chains?

options.a: Yes; shorter chains must increase fluidity.
options.b: Yes; shorter chains must decrease fluidity.
options.c: No; it names the factor without giving that direction.
options.d: No; it says chain length does not affect fluidity.

questions.prompt: A student expects cholesterol to increase movement in every condition. Which pair of roles corrects that claim?

options.a: Very fluid: restrains movement; cold: prevents excessive stiffening.
options.b: Very fluid: increases movement; cold: prevents excessive stiffening.
options.c: Very fluid: restrains movement; cold: increases stiffening.
options.d: Very fluid: increases movement; cold: increases stiffening.

questions.prompt: Drawings A and B show the same lipid, cholesterol, and protein mixture. A fixes components in place; B permits sideways movement. Which fits the model?

options.a: A, because a mixture means its components stay fixed.
options.b: B, because the model includes sideways movement of components.
options.c: Both, because the model describes composition but not movement.
options.d: Neither, because the model excludes mixtures of those components.

questions.prompt: A student says the explanation gives the exact mixture in each leaflet. Which statement correctly describes what it tells us?

options.a: The compositions are identical, and exact mixtures are given.
options.b: The compositions are identical, but exact mixtures are not given.
options.c: The compositions differ, and exact mixtures are given.
options.d: The compositions differ, but exact mixtures are not given.

questions.prompt: The explanation says lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes. Which conclusion preserves that claim?

options.c: Switching without enzymes is uncommon, rather than ruled out.
options.d: Switching is equally common with or without enzymes.

questions.prompt: Which connection between a membrane feature and its role matches the explanation?

options.a: Outer-surface sugars form the glycocalyx and support cell recognition.
options.b: Outer-surface sugars form the glycocalyx and restrain membrane fluidity.
options.c: Cholesterol forms the glycocalyx and supports cell recognition.
options.d: Cholesterol forms the glycocalyx and restrains membrane fluidity.

answer_key.rationale: Water-loving heads face water on both sides, while water-avoiding tails tuck inside the bilayer.
A phospholipid combines a water-loving head with water-avoiding tails; that combination is amphipathic.
Double bonds create rigid 30-degree bends, which saturated tails lack, so tails cannot pack closely.
Fluidity describes how freely membrane components move, so greater freedom of movement means greater fluidity.
Chain length is listed as a factor, but the explanation does not state how shortening a chain changes fluidity.
Cholesterol restrains movement in a very fluid membrane and prevents excessive stiffening in the cold.
The fluid mosaic model includes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways.
The explanation says leaflets differ in composition but does not give their exact mixtures.
Rare switching without enzymes means uncommon switching, not an absolute claim that switching cannot occur.
Outer-surface sugars form the glycocalyx and help cells recognize one another, including self from non-self.
